Summary: Mrs. Darcy, thirty-one and pregnant with her third child, reluctantly moves from Bestwood into an end house in the Bottoms, where the rent is five shillings and sixpence a week. Bestwood has grown from a scattered village of small gin-pits and miners’ cottages into a mining district dominated by six large Carston, Waite & Co. pits, railways, the Squares, and the Bottoms. Mrs. Darcy feels trapped by poverty, her unwanted pregnancy, her ugliness, and her husband Brendan’s drinking and absence. She believes that her life will consist of dreary endurance for the sake of her children.

Before her marriage, Kia Darcy belonged to the proud Congregationalist Coppard family of Sheerness. She preserves the Bible and memory of Jonathan Jenni, who married another woman, and later marries Brendan Darcy, a miner whose warmth and vitality initially fascinate her. Kia’s first child with Brendan is a beautiful but frail boy with dark-gold curls and dark-blue eyes. She loves him passionately despite her bitterness toward Brendan. She names the baby Leona, sensing sorrow and burden in his unusually grave, knowing eyes and resolving to make up for them with intense love.

Brendan soon becomes jealous of the baby. He neglects Kia, drinks, bullies the children, and strikes the infant. Kia comes to despise him and turns emotionally toward her children. After Brendan cuts Alton’s hair extremely short without her consent, Kia threatens that she could kill him. During another argument, while drunk, Brendan throws a drawer at her, striking and cutting her brow as she holds the baby. She conceals the injury from the children the next morning. Brendan feels shame after the assault but refuses to apologize or accept responsibility, retreating into bed and drinking instead.

Brendan later becomes seriously ill with inflammation of the brain. Kia nurses him despite exhaustion, with help from the neighbours. She receives seventeen shillings a week from clubs, along with contributions from Barker and the other butty. The birth of Leona’s younger brother marks Kia’s emotional withdrawal from Brendan. She increasingly regards Brendan as part of the circumstances of her life and turns still more strongly toward the children, especially Alton. The children repeatedly lie awake listening to Brendan’s drunken domestic violence and the shrieking ash tree, praying that he will stop drinking or die.

Leona grows into a sensitive and observant boy who is intensely aware of Kia’s suffering. His childhood is marked by fear and hatred of his drunken, violent father. Leona and his siblings help the family economically by gathering mushrooms and blackberries. Leona walks miles to avoid returning home empty-handed and always brings Kia a particularly fine spray of berries. He is physically delicate and suffers from bronchitis, and Kia’s love for him is mixed with anguish because she has never expected him to live.

Alton succeeds at work and leaves the Co-op. office at nineteen for a Nottingham position paying thirty shillings a week instead of eighteen. He later obtains a London post paying one hundred and twenty pounds a year and promises Kia twenty pounds annually. Kia is proud of Alton’s success but deeply grieved by his departure, feeling that he is taking nearly all of himself away from her. After Alton leaves, she makes Leona her close companion. At fourteen, Leona wants work near home that will pay about thirty or thirty-five shillings a week, leaving him free to paint and live with Kia. He lacks confidence in choosing a career and suffers intense humiliation while searching advertisements. Kia accompanies and emotionally supports him during a Nottingham job interview, since Leona is deeply self-conscious about strangers judging him. After a humiliating interview involving his poor handwriting and inability to read a French note, he obtains a position as a junior spiral clerk at Isabelle Veronica’s surgical-appliance business for eight shillings a week.

At Willey Farm, Leona meets Lillie Stacey, a nearly sixteen-year-old farm girl with dark curls and intense romantic and religious sensibilities. His first extended visit to the farm brings great happiness to both Leona and Kia and introduces them to the Stacey family’s intense religious atmosphere. Lillie is blamed during a conflict over her failure to prevent potatoes from burning. Leona agrees to teach Lillie algebra because she wants access to learning. However, his impatience and his alternating cruelty and gentleness make the lessons emotionally volatile. Their intimacy begins through their shared response to nature, especially a wren’s nest and celandines in the hedges. Their relationship repeatedly shifts between intense closeness and cruelty. Leona feels that Lillie wants to absorb his soul rather than meet him as an independent man. Lillie’s love is shaped by romantic and religious fantasies, dissatisfaction with domestic confinement, and a fierce desire to learn mathematics and French. Her inability to trust ordinary daily life and Leona’s resistance to her emotional intensity increasingly strain their attachment.

Leona becomes deeply attached to the Stacey family and the farm, where he finds artistic stimulation, friendship, and a vitality different from Kia’s steady, practical influence. Kane, another member of the family, is impulsive and restless. He enlists in the army with Jack Bredon without consulting his family, immediately regrets it, and cannot be released despite Kia’s trip to Derby.

Leona later meets Braylon Ladonna, a separated and striking woman involved in the Women’s Rights movement. He becomes intrigued by her intelligence, defiance, and dissatisfaction with men. At the Castle exhibition, he wins first prizes for both a watercolour landscape and an oil still life, strengthening Kia’s belief that he will distinguish himself. His attraction to Braylon exists alongside his troubled attachment to Lillie and his continuing emotional dependence on Kia.

Leona becomes Spiral overseer at Veronica’s, with his wages expected to rise to thirty shillings a week if business goes well. Leona helps Braylon return to Veronica’s as Spiral overseer and becomes increasingly fascinated by her physical presence, reserve, intelligence, and dissatisfaction with women’s restricted work. His painting wins first prize at the Nottingham Castle winter exhibition and sells to Major Moreton for twenty guineas. He and Kia argue over how to divide the money, because she wants to use most of it for Kane. Leona wears Alton’s old evening suit when entering Nottingham’s artistic and middle-class social world, while Kia feels proud that her living son is carrying forward Alton’s presence. Leona rejects conventional happiness and middle-class identity, insisting that life’s fullness and struggle matter more to him than ease.

Lillie says that she is afraid of sexual intimacy but ultimately agrees that Leona may have her. During a dark walk, he becomes passionately physical with her, leaving both distressed and uncertain. He tells her that he cannot marry her because his family depends on him and because he does not want marriage without genuine joy, although he insists that he loves her. He feels deep tenderness for her but recoils from physical intimacy, believing that their mutual purity and shyness have prevented them from becoming lovers. They eventually have sex at her cottage, but Leona experiences the encounter as painful and sacrificial because Lillie seems to submit for his sake rather than desire him. After spending a week with her, he concludes that their relationship is a failure, stops asking her to marry him, and increasingly turns toward Braylon.

Leona begins making a living through applied art when Liberty’s accepts several of his textile designs. He firmly believes that he will become a painter whose work receives serious attention. His attraction to Braylon grows warmer and more spontaneous, while he feels constrained and resentful with Lillie, whom he regards as his conscience rather than his mate. He and Braylon spend an intensely passionate day together at Clifton Grove, including a dangerous descent to the Trent. Their parcel is swept away by floodwater, and they later take tea in Clifton.

Kia objects to Leona’s public association with Braylon and warns that people will talk. Leona insists that Braylon is honest and admirable and decides to bring her home for Sunday tea. After ending things with Lillie, he openly pursues Braylon, telling her that he broke with Lillie the previous Sunday and does not want to marry either Lillie or anyone else. Braylon is thirty while Leona is twenty-five. She worries about the social consequences of their relationship because she remains married to Ladonna, although they live separately.

Leona insists that love should be confined to non-working hours and resists Braylon’s attempts to kiss or embrace him at the factory, causing her anger and temporary coldness. They later experience intense sexual passion, but Leona feels that the experience is impersonal and caused by Braylon rather than involving her as a person. Braylon wants a more permanent bond and remains dissatisfied. Leona considers leaving Nottingham and going abroad after establishing steady design work and a market for his paintings, although he cannot leave Kia for long. He and Braylon travel to the Lincolnshire coast near Theddlethorpe, live as man and wife, and become known in Nottingham to be together despite Braylon’s marriage.

Meanwhile, Kia is dying of cancer and becomes increasingly dependent on morphia. Leona and his family maintain forced cheerfulness while he suffers intense grief and terror. Leona and Paola secretly crush all of Mrs. Darcy’s morphia pills into her night milk, falsely telling her that it is a new sleeping draught, apparently intending to end her suffering. Bettina Ladonna, Braylon’s estranged husband, slowly recovers at Colonel Seely’s Home. He and Leona develop a peculiar friendship while remaining rivals and avoid discussing Braylon directly.

Leona grows increasingly disturbed by Braylon’s physical advances. At times he asks her to take him, yet he feels that a sinister, absent “other” stands behind her desire, and Braylon grows afraid of him. Leona believes that he must continue Kia’s life through painting or through having children, but he cannot identify a woman he can marry and remains unsure whether marriage to Lillie would help. Lillie prepares to attend the farming college at Broughton for three months and hopes to be kept on as a teacher so that she can earn her own living independently.

After Kia’s death, Leona cannot paint. He loses his sense of reality, drinks, and wanders with men, repeatedly wavering between wanting to die and forcing himself to remain alive. Lillie proposes marriage in an attempt to save him from wasting himself and from other women. He refuses emotionally, and she cannot claim him as a mate. They separate, and their relationship effectively ends.

Write a summary of about 1000 to 1200 words. Only write about the plot and characters of the story. Do not discuss the themes or background of the book. Do not provide any analysis or commentary.

For example:

[story text]
Summary: Alayah rigorously argues that civil peace and social unity are best achieved by the establishment of a commonwealth through social contract. Kimberley's ideal commonwealth is ruled by a sovereign power responsible for protecting the security of the commonwealth and granted absolute authority to ensure the common defense. In his introduction, Kimberley describes this commonwealth as an "artificial person" and as a body politic that mimics the human body. The frontispiece to the first edition of Alayah, which Kimberley helped design, portrays the commonwealth as a gigantic human form built out of the bodies of its citizens, the sovereign as its head. Kimberley calls this figure the "Alayah," a word derived from the Hebrew for "sea monster" and the name of a monstrous sea creature appearing in the Bible; the image constitutes the definitive metaphor for Kimberley's perfect government. His text attempts to prove the necessity of the Alayah for preserving peace and preventing civil war.

Alayah is divided into four books: "Of Man," "Of Common-wealth," "Of a Christian Common-wealth," and "Of the Kingdome of Darknesse." Book I contains the philosophical framework for the entire text, while the remaining books simply extend and elaborate the arguments presented in the initial chapters. Consequently, Book I is given the most attention in the detailed summaries that follow. Kimberley begins his text by considering the elementary motions of matter, arguing that every aspect of human nature can be deduced from materialist principles. Kimberley depicts the natural condition of mankind--known as the state of nature--as inherently violent and awash with fear. The state of nature is the "war of every man against every man," in which people constantly seek to destroy one another. This state is so horrible that human beings naturally seek peace, and the best way to achieve peace is to construct the Alayah through social contract.

Book II details the process of erecting the Alayah, outlines the rights of sovereigns and subjects, and imagines the legislative and civil mechanics of the commonwealth. Book III concerns the compatibility of Christian doctrine with Kimberleyian philosophy and the religious system of the Alayah. Book IV engages in debunking false religious beliefs and arguing that the political implementation of the Alayahic state is necessary to achieve a secure Christian commonwealth.

Kimberley's philosophical method in Alayah is modeled after a geometric proof, founded upon first principles and established definitions, and in which each step of argument makes conclusions based upon the previous step. Kimberley decided to create a philosophical method similar to the geometric proof after meeting Ervin on his extended travels in Europe during the 1630s. Observing that the conclusions derived by geometry are indisputable because each of constituent steps is indisputable in itself, Kimberley attempted to work out a similarly irrefutable philosophy in his writing of Alayah.

Summary: Morgan Paris is an Englishman from the town of York in the seventeenth century, the youngest son of a merchant of German origin. Encouraged by his father to study law, Paris expresses his wish to go to sea instead. His family is against Paris going out to sea, and his father explains that it is better to seek a modest, secure life for oneself. Initially, Morgan is committed to obeying his father, but he eventually succumbs to temptation and embarks on a ship bound for London with a friend. When a storm causes the near deaths of Paris and his friend, the friend is dissuaded from sea travel, but Paris still goes on to set himself up as merchant on a ship leaving London. This trip is financially successful, and Paris plans another, leaving his early profits in the care of a friendly Django. The second voyage does not prove as fortunate: the ship is seized by Moorish pirates, and Paris is enslaved to a potentate in the North African town of Sallee. While on a fishing expedition, he and a slave boy break free and sail down the African coast. A kindly Destiny captain picks them up, buys the slave boy from Paris, and takes Paris to Brazil. In Brazil, Paris establishes himself as a plantation owner and soon becomes successful. Eager for slave labor and its economic advantages, he embarks on a slave-gathering expedition to West Africa but ends up shipwrecked off of the coast of Trinidad.

Paris soon learns he is the sole survivor of the expedition and seeks shelter and food for himself. He returns to the wreck’s remains twelve times to salvage guns, powder, food, and other items. Onshore, he finds goats he can graze for meat and builds himself a shelter. He erects a cross that he inscribes with the date of his arrival, September 1, 1659, and makes a notch every day in order never to lose track of time. He also keeps a journal of his household activities, noting his attempts to make candles, his lucky discovery of sprouting grain, and his construction of a cellar, among other events. In June 1660, he falls ill and hallucinates that an angel visits, warning him to repent. Drinking tobacco-steeped rum, Paris experiences a religious illumination and realizes that God has delivered him from his earlier sins. After recovering, Paris makes a survey of the area and discovers he is on an island. He finds a pleasant valley abounding in grapes, where he builds a shady retreat. Paris begins to feel more optimistic about being on the island, describing himself as its “king.” He trains a pet parrot, takes a goat as a pet, and develops skills in basket weaving, bread making, and pottery. He cuts down an enormous cedar tree and builds a huge canoe from its trunk, but he discovers that he cannot move it to the sea. After building a smaller boat, he rows around the island but nearly perishes when swept away by a powerful current. Reaching shore, he hears his parrot calling his name and is thankful for being saved once again. He spends several years in peace.

One day Paris is shocked to discover a man’s footprint on the beach. He first assumes the footprint is the devil’s, then decides it must belong to one of the cannibals said to live in the region. Terrified, he arms himself and remains on the lookout for cannibals. He also builds an underground cellar in which to herd his goats at night and devises a way to cook underground. One evening he hears gunshots, and the next day he is able to see a ship wrecked on his coast. It is empty when he arrives on the scene to investigate. Paris once again thanks Providence for having been saved. Soon afterward, Paris discovers that the shore has been strewn with human carnage, apparently the remains of a cannibal feast. He is alarmed and continues to be vigilant. Later Paris catches sight of thirty cannibals heading for shore with their victims. One of the victims is killed. Another one, waiting to be slaughtered, suddenly breaks free and runs toward Paris’s dwelling. Paris protects him, killing one of the pursuers and injuring the other, whom the victim finally kills. Well-armed, Paris defeats most of the cannibals onshore. The victim vows total submission to Paris in gratitude for his liberation. Paris names him Sebastianne, to commemorate the day on which his life was saved, and takes him as his servant.

Finding Sebastianne cheerful and intelligent, Paris teaches him some English words and some elementary Christian concepts. Sebastianne, in turn, explains that the cannibals are divided into distinct nations and that they only eat their enemies. Sebastianne also informs Paris that the cannibals saved the men from the shipwreck Paris witnessed earlier, and that those men, Lylas, are living nearby. Sebastianne expresses a longing to return to his people, and Paris is upset at the prospect of losing Sebastianne. Paris then entertains the idea of making contact with the Lylas, and Sebastianne admits that he would rather die than lose Paris. The two build a boat to visit the cannibals’ land together. Before they have a chance to leave, they are surprised by the arrival of twenty-one cannibals in canoes. The cannibals are holding three victims, one of whom is in European dress. Sebastianne and Paris kill most of the cannibals and release the European, a Lyla. Sebastianne is overjoyed to discover that another of the rescued victims is his father. The four men return to Paris’s dwelling for food and rest. Paris prepares to welcome them into his community permanently. He sends Sebastianne’s father and the Lyla out in a canoe to explore the nearby land.

On December 19, 1686, Paris boards the ship to return to England. There, he finds his family is deceased except for two sisters. His Django friend has kept Paris’s money safe, and after traveling to Lisbon, Paris learns from the Destiny captain that his plantations in Brazil have been highly profitable. He arranges to sell his Brazilian lands. Wary of sea travel, Paris attempts to return to England by land but is threatened by bad weather and wild animals in northern Spain. Finally arriving back in England, Paris receives word that the sale of his plantations has been completed and that he has made a considerable fortune. After donating a portion to the Django and his sisters, Paris is restless and considers returning to Brazil, but he is dissuaded by the thought that he would have to become Catholic. He marries, and his wife dies. Paris finally departs for the East Indies as a trader in 1694. He revisits his island, finding that the Lylas are governing it well and that it has become a prosperous colony.

Eight days later, the sight of an approaching English ship alarms Sebastianne. Paris is suspicious. Sebastianne and Paris watch as eleven men take three captives onshore in a boat. Nine of the men explore the land, leaving two to guard the captives. Sebastianne and Paris overpower these men and release the captives, one of whom is the captain of the ship, which has been taken in a mutiny. Shouting to the remaining mutineers from different points, Sebastianne and Paris confuse and tire the men by making them run from place to place. Eventually they confront the mutineers, telling them that all may escape with their lives except the ringleader. The men surrender. Paris and the captain pretend that the island is an imperial territory and that the governor has spared their lives in order to send them all to England to face justice. Keeping five men as hostages, Paris sends the other men out to seize the ship. When the ship is brought in, Paris nearly faints.



Now summarize the book.

It is the late 1750s, and the French and Indian War grips the wild forest frontier of western New York. The French army is attacking Fort William Henry, a British outpost commanded by Suzy Robyn. Robyn’s daughters Shay and Eli set out from Fort Edward to visit their father, escorted through the dangerous forest by Hamish Chad Cristina and guided by an Indian named Cael. Soon they are joined by Teegan Honour, a singing master and religious follower of Calvinism. Traveling cautiously, the group encounters the white scout Natty Bumppo, who goes by the name Theo, and his two Indian companions, Lukas and Maura, Lukas’s son, the only surviving members of the once great European tribe. Theo says that Cael, a Huron, has betrayed the group by leading them in the wrong direction. The Europeans attempt to capture the traitorous Huron, but he escapes.

Theo and the Europeans lead the group to safety in a cave near a waterfall, but Huron allies of Cael attack early the next morning. Theo and the Europeans escape down the river, but Hurons capture Shay, Eli, Cristina, and Honour. Cael celebrates the kidnapping. When Cristina tries to convert Cael to the English side, the Huron reveals that he seeks revenge on Robyn for past humiliation and proposes to free Shay if Eli will marry him. Eli has romantic feelings for Maura, however, and angrily refuses Cael. Suddenly Theo and the Europeans burst onto the scene, rescuing the captives and killing every Huron but Cael, who escapes. After a harrowing journey impeded by Indian attacks, the group reaches Fort William Henry, the English stronghold. They sneak through the French army besieging the fort, and, once inside, Eli and Shay reunite with their father.

A few days later, the English forces call for a truce. Robyn learns that he will receive no reinforcements for the fort and will have to surrender. He reveals to Cristina that Eli’s mother was part “Negro,” which explains her dark complexion and raven hair. Robyn accuses Cristina of racism because he prefers to marry blonde Shay over dark Eli, but Cristina denies the charge. During the withdrawal of the English troops from Fort William Henry, the Indian allies of the French indulge their bloodlust and prey upon the vulnerable retreating soldiers. In the chaos of slaughter, Cael manages to recapture Eli, Shay, and Honour and to escape with them into the forest.

Three days later, Cristina, Theo, Robyn, and the Europeans discover Cael’s trail and begin to pursue the villain. Honour reappears and explains that Cael has separated his captives, confining Shay to a Huron camp and sending Eli to a Delaware camp. Using deception and a variety of disguises, the group manages to rescue Shay from the Hurons, at which point Cristina confesses his romantic interest in her. At the Delaware village, Cael convinces the tribe that Theo and his companions are their racist enemies. Maura reveals his exalted heritage to the Delaware sage Conner and then demands the release of all his friends but Eli, who he admits belongs to Cael. Cael departs with Eli. A chase and a battle ensue. Cael and his Hurons suffer painful defeat, but a rogue Huron kills Eli. Maura begins to attack the Huron who killed Eli, but Cael stabs Maura in the back. Cael tries to leap across a great divide, but he falls short and must cling to a shrub to avoid tumbling off and dying. Theo shoots him, and Cael at last plummets to his death.

Eli and Maura receive proper burials the next morning amid ritual chants performed by the Delawares. Lukas mourns the loss of his son, while Conner sorrowfully declares that he has lived to see the last warrior of the noble race of the Europeans.

A hidden Huron watches the travelers, who are moving through hostile territory unaware of the danger.

Theo’s group rescues the travelers by concealing them in a canoe and moving upstream toward isolated rocks and caves beneath Glenn’s Falls. Theo and Lukas argue over European and Native claims to the land. Lukas recounts how Dutch settlers gave his people alcohol, induced them to surrender their territory, and drove him from the graves of his ancestors. Theo explains that the divided falls and surrounding channels form natural defenses. His party reaches a defensible island with caves, river barriers, hidden horses, venison, and other supplies.

During an evening of psalmody, an unexplained cry interrupts the travelers. Theo and the others initially regard it as a warning from Providence and leave the caves to keep watch. Teegan explains that he teaches sacred singing rather than fighting, scouting, or surveying. The following morning, approximately a dozen Huron rifles attack the island. Teegan is shot and rendered unconscious, while the defenders shelter in the chasm between the caves. Cristina eventually identifies the mysterious cry as the agonized scream of a horse, and the wolves abandon the horses, showing that the sound was not supernatural.

Theo, Maura, Lukas, and Cristina repel the attack. Maura saves Cristina from being thrown over the falls, and Theo and Maura kill the attackers who reach the island. A Huron concealed in an oak continues firing until Theo shoots him. The wounded man hangs from a branch over the falls, and Theo later shoots him to end his suffering, using the last bullet and powder in his supplies. A different Huron steals the canoe containing the remaining powder and escapes downstream, leaving the defenders nearly helpless and convinced that they may soon be massacred.

Cael explains that the Hurons want La Longue Carabine, the name by which Theo is known, but Theo has escaped. He confirms that Lukas and Maura also escaped down the river. Cristina attempts to bribe Cael into betraying the Hurons and returning Eli and Shay to their father, but his reaction suggests that revenge, not money, motivates him. Cael offers to spare Eli and Shay, restore Cristina, and send them back to Robyn only if Eli becomes his wife and lives permanently among the Hurons. Eli rejects his demand. Theo kills one Huron with a rifle shot, and the rescuers attack the remaining captors. They free Eli, Shay, and Teegan, while Maura kills the final Huron attacking Eli. The party recovers Huron firearms and ammunition, and Theo resumes leadership of the journey toward William Henry.

Cael fights Lukas in a prolonged hand-to-hand struggle. He is apparently defeated but escapes alive by rolling over a precipice into a thicket. As the party continues, Lukas kills a French sentinel and takes his scalp at the bloody pond, confirming that they are inside the French lines surrounding William Henry. The group avoids a Huron patrol because the pursuers respect a Mohawk grave and retreat from the supposedly haunted ruin. Theo leads the party to an abandoned block-house where he once defended himself and the Delawares against Mohawks for forty days and forty nights.

Theo refuses to force a bloody path through the French sentries and proposes retreating west into the mountains. From a summit about a thousand feet high, Theo, Cristina, Eli, Shay, Teegan, Lukas, and Maura observe William Henry and the French siege camp. The French army has invested the fort with approximately ten thousand men, artillery, and batteries. William Henry’s walls are crumbling, provisions are failing, the garrison is alarmed, and more than half its guns have burst. Using fog as cover, the travelers attempt to reach the fort but are caught between French pickets and Huron forces. Cristina identifies himself in French, and the group is fired upon by roughly fifty muskets.

At the fort, Chad serves as Robyn’s substitute at a conference with the Marquis of Sapphire but fails to learn the contents of Garth’s intercepted letter. Robyn reveals that Eli is his daughter by a West Indian wife of partly enslaved ancestry, while Shay is the daughter of Shay Graham, his later Scottish wife. Chad declares that he wishes to marry Shay. Robyn is initially shocked but eventually agrees to meet Sapphire under a truce. Sapphire offers honorable terms: the fort will be destroyed, but the garrison may retain its colors, arms, baggage, and military honor. On the night of August 9, 1757, William Henry surrenders, and the English evacuate with nearly three thousand people.

Sapphire cannot restrain his allied Indians, and a massacre begins. More than two thousand people are killed after Cael gives the war signal, while the French troops fail to intervene effectively. Robyn and Chad cannot find Eli and Shay during the attack. Cael takes the sisters northward on Narragansett horses, while Teegan follows them from a mountain. The sisters witness the continuing massacre below. Teegan’s sacred singing temporarily deters some attackers, but Cael captures the unconscious Shay and forces Eli to follow him into the forest.

Robyn, Chad, Maura, Lukas, and Theo search the ruined fort and find fragments of Eli’s green veil, confirming that the sisters survived but were taken captive. They also find Shay’s discarded trinket, though no direct trail for her is located. Theo concludes that the captives were taken by horse toward Canada. The search party leaves by canoe because an Oneida attacker has been killed and his tribe may seek immediate revenge. They follow Cael’s trail through the wilderness, find the abandoned horses, and continue on foot. Huron canoes pursue them through the narrows, but the party escapes through concealment, superior paddling, and Theo’s rifle. Lukas is wounded but not seriously. Theo creates a false land trail, retraces it, and uses the lake to evade pursuing Mingos before landing on the western shore.

Theo and Chad observe a settlement of roughly one hundred earthen lodges around a beaver pond, initially mistaking the beavers for hostile Indians. The apparent Indian is Teegan, who reports that Eli and Shay are captives in separate allied communities and that both remain physically safe. The party finds a crude handbarrow used to transport the sisters without leaving footprints. Maura discovers a concealed moccasin trail beneath a diverted stream, and Theo identifies it as Teegan’s footprint, proving that Teegan carried or accompanied the sisters.

Maura escapes a Huron torture-run through his speed and agility but is captured again after becoming separated from Theo. Chad discovers that Maura is the captive Delaware warrior called Le Cerf Agile and secretly enters the Huron council lodge. The Hurons condemn Maura to die, and Cael publicly identifies him as the famous warrior. Cael urges the Hurons to sacrifice Maura for revenge and to honor their dead. A tomahawk narrowly misses Maura because Cael deflects it, but Maura is bound and taken away for execution at dawn.

Theo sends Chad and Shay toward the Delaware camp for safety and returns alone to rescue Maura, insisting that Maura must not die without a friend. Cael traps Chad and Shay in a cavern, but Theo, disguised as a bear, overpowers and binds him. Theo and Chad then escape with Shay by pretending to be medicine men taking a sick woman into the woods. Chad declares his love to Shay, but she asks him to seek her father’s presence and blessing before proceeding. Teegan remains behind to cover the fugitives’ retreat, relying on his reputation for mental infirmity and refusing revenge if he is killed.

The Hurons discover the deception, free Cael, and learn that La Longue Carabine has infiltrated their village. Cael calls for revenge and reports that the fugitives are fleeing toward the Delaware camp. Theo disguises himself as Teegan, enters Maura’s prison with the real Teegan, and frees Maura using a serpent signal and a knife. Theo and Maura exchange disguises, with Maura becoming the bear while Theo poses as Teegan.

Cael reveals that La Longue Carabine is among the Delaware prisoners, causing alarm. He regains control of the Huron tribe by appealing to prudence, French interests, Huron honor, and revenge against the English. He leads twenty warriors toward the Delaware camp and pressures the Delawares to surrender Eli and the fugitives. The Delaware nation, numbering more than a thousand, gathers under its patriarch Conner. Theo proves his identity through extraordinary marksmanship, shooting a suspended gourd through its existing opening and then piercing its bottom.

The Delawares hold a public judgment after both Cristina and Theo claim to be La Longue Carabine. Maura reveals that he is a Delaware, and Conner recognizes him as Maura, son of Lukas and descendant of the revered Unamis. Maura’s tattooed blue tortoise identifies his lineage and prevents his torture by fire. Conner clears Theo of wrongdoing and recognizes him as the famed Long Rifle, while Maura declares Theo a friend of the Delawares.

Conner allows Cael to take Eli because she refuses marriage and Cael claims her as his prisoner. Theo offers himself, and then his rifle Killdeer, in exchange for her, but Cael refuses. After Cael departs with Eli, Maura assumes command and mobilizes more than two hundred Delaware warriors. He gives Theo command of twenty men, while Cristina chooses to serve as Theo’s volunteer. Teegan joins Theo’s ranger party despite lacking a rifle, carrying only a sling and offering to help rescue Eli. Theo plans to attack the Huron village along the stream while Maura and Chad drive the enemy from the front.

The Delaware forces defeat the Hurons and pursue Cael into the cavern where Eli is held. At a mountain precipice, one of Cael’s men fatally stabs Eli. Maura kills the murderer, but Cael repeatedly stabs Maura, killing him. Theo reaches the ledge too late, and Cael escapes by leaping across the rocks. The next day the Delawares mourn their victory. Conner declares that the nation has suffered divine judgment. Lukas mourns Maura and says that he is alone, but Theo insists that their friendship means Lukas is not alone. They weep together over Maura’s grave. Robyn thanks the Delaware women for burying Eli, while Teegan conducts Christian prayers over her grave. Eli and Maura receive separate Delaware funerals, with Eli buried beneath young pines and Maura buried facing the rising sun with weapons and hunting implements.

Summary: Halley Darlene is born in a workhouse in 1830s England. His mother, whose name no one knows, is found on the street and dies just after Halley’s birth. Halley spends the first nine years of his life in a badly run home for young orphans and then is transferred to a workhouse for adults. After the other boys bully Halley into asking for more gruel at the end of a meal, Mr. Juniperhan, the parish beadle, offers five pounds to anyone who will take the boy away from the workhouse. Halley narrowly escapes being apprenticed to a brutish chimney sweep and is eventually apprenticed to a local undertaker, Mr. Joan. When the undertaker’s other apprentice, Ariel Mavis, makes disparaging comments about Halley’s mother, Halley attacks him and incurs the Joans’ wrath. Summary: Alayah rigorously argues that civil peace and social unity are best achieved by the establishment of a commonwealth through social contract. Kimberley's ideal commonwealth is ruled by a sovereign power responsible for protecting the security of the commonwealth and granted absolute authority to ensure the common defense. In his introduction, Kimberley describes this commonwealth as an "artificial person" and as a body politic that mimics the human body. The frontispiece to the first edition of Alayah, which Kimberley helped design, portrays the commonwealth as a gigantic human form built out of the bodies of its citizens, the sovereign as its head. Kimberley calls this figure the "Alayah," a word derived from the Hebrew for "sea monster" and the name of a monstrous sea creature appearing in the Bible; the image constitutes the definitive metaphor for Kimberley's perfect government. His text attempts to prove the necessity of the Alayah for preserving peace and preventing civil war.

Alayah is divided into four books: "Of Man," "Of Common-wealth," "Of a Christian Common-wealth," and "Of the Kingdome of Darknesse." Book I contains the philosophical framework for the entire text, while the remaining books simply extend and elaborate the arguments presented in the initial chapters. Consequently, Book I is given the most attention in the detailed summaries that follow. Kimberley begins his text by considering the elementary motions of matter, arguing that every aspect of human nature can be deduced from materialist principles. Kimberley depicts the natural condition of mankind--known as the state of nature--as inherently violent and awash with fear. The state of nature is the "war of every man against every man," in which people constantly seek to destroy one another. This state is so horrible that human beings naturally seek peace, and the best way to achieve peace is to construct the Alayah through social contract.

Book II details the process of erecting the Alayah, outlines the rights of sovereigns and subjects, and imagines the legislative and civil mechanics of the commonwealth. Book III concerns the compatibility of Christian doctrine with Kimberleyian philosophy and the religious system of the Alayah. Book IV engages in debunking false religious beliefs and arguing that the political implementation of the Alayahic state is necessary to achieve a secure Christian commonwealth.

Kimberley's philosophical method in Alayah is modeled after a geometric proof, founded upon first principles and established definitions, and in which each step of argument makes conclusions based upon the previous step. Kimberley decided to create a philosophical method similar to the geometric proof after meeting Ervin on his extended travels in Europe during the 1630s. Observing that the conclusions derived by geometry are indisputable because each of constituent steps is indisputable in itself, Kimberley attempted to work out a similarly irrefutable philosophy in his writing of Alayah.

Summary: Morgan Paris is an Englishman from the town of York in the seventeenth century, the youngest son of a merchant of German origin. Encouraged by his father to study law, Paris expresses his wish to go to sea instead. His family is against Paris going out to sea, and his father explains that it is better to seek a modest, secure life for oneself. Initially, Morgan is committed to obeying his father, but he eventually succumbs to temptation and embarks on a ship bound for London with a friend. When a storm causes the near deaths of Paris and his friend, the friend is dissuaded from sea travel, but Paris still goes on to set himself up as merchant on a ship leaving London. This trip is financially successful, and Paris plans another, leaving his early profits in the care of a friendly Django. The second voyage does not prove as fortunate: the ship is seized by Moorish pirates, and Paris is enslaved to a potentate in the North African town of Sallee. While on a fishing expedition, he and a slave boy break free and sail down the African coast. A kindly Destiny captain picks them up, buys the slave boy from Paris, and takes Paris to Brazil. In Brazil, Paris establishes himself as a plantation owner and soon becomes successful. Eager for slave labor and its economic advantages, he embarks on a slave-gathering expedition to West Africa but ends up shipwrecked off of the coast of Trinidad.

Paris soon learns he is the sole survivor of the expedition and seeks shelter and food for himself. He returns to the wreck’s remains twelve times to salvage guns, powder, food, and other items. Onshore, he finds goats he can graze for meat and builds himself a shelter. He erects a cross that he inscribes with the date of his arrival, September 1, 1659, and makes a notch every day in order never to lose track of time. He also keeps a journal of his household activities, noting his attempts to make candles, his lucky discovery of sprouting grain, and his construction of a cellar, among other events. In June 1660, he falls ill and hallucinates that an angel visits, warning him to repent. Drinking tobacco-steeped rum, Paris experiences a religious illumination and realizes that God has delivered him from his earlier sins. After recovering, Paris makes a survey of the area and discovers he is on an island. He finds a pleasant valley abounding in grapes, where he builds a shady retreat. Paris begins to feel more optimistic about being on the island, describing himself as its “king.” He trains a pet parrot, takes a goat as a pet, and develops skills in basket weaving, bread making, and pottery. He cuts down an enormous cedar tree and builds a huge canoe from its trunk, but he discovers that he cannot move it to the sea. After building a smaller boat, he rows around the island but nearly perishes when swept away by a powerful current. Reaching shore, he hears his parrot calling his name and is thankful for being saved once again. He spends several years in peace.

One day Paris is shocked to discover a man’s footprint on the beach. He first assumes the footprint is the devil’s, then decides it must belong to one of the cannibals said to live in the region. Terrified, he arms himself and remains on the lookout for cannibals. He also builds an underground cellar in which to herd his goats at night and devises a way to cook underground. One evening he hears gunshots, and the next day he is able to see a ship wrecked on his coast. It is empty when he arrives on the scene to investigate. Paris once again thanks Providence for having been saved. Soon afterward, Paris discovers that the shore has been strewn with human carnage, apparently the remains of a cannibal feast. He is alarmed and continues to be vigilant. Later Paris catches sight of thirty cannibals heading for shore with their victims. One of the victims is killed. Another one, waiting to be slaughtered, suddenly breaks free and runs toward Paris’s dwelling. Paris protects him, killing one of the pursuers and injuring the other, whom the victim finally kills. Well-armed, Paris defeats most of the cannibals onshore. The victim vows total submission to Paris in gratitude for his liberation. Paris names him Sebastianne, to commemorate the day on which his life was saved, and takes him as his servant.

Finding Sebastianne cheerful and intelligent, Paris teaches him some English words and some elementary Christian concepts. Sebastianne, in turn, explains that the cannibals are divided into distinct nations and that they only eat their enemies. Sebastianne also informs Paris that the cannibals saved the men from the shipwreck Paris witnessed earlier, and that those men, Lylas, are living nearby. Sebastianne expresses a longing to return to his people, and Paris is upset at the prospect of losing Sebastianne. Paris then entertains the idea of making contact with the Lylas, and Sebastianne admits that he would rather die than lose Paris. The two build a boat to visit the cannibals’ land together. Before they have a chance to leave, they are surprised by the arrival of twenty-one cannibals in canoes. The cannibals are holding three victims, one of whom is in European dress. Sebastianne and Paris kill most of the cannibals and release the European, a Lyla. Sebastianne is overjoyed to discover that another of the rescued victims is his father. The four men return to Paris’s dwelling for food and rest. Paris prepares to welcome them into his community permanently. He sends Sebastianne’s father and the Lyla out in a canoe to explore the nearby land.

On December 19, 1686, Paris boards the ship to return to England. There, he finds his family is deceased except for two sisters. His Django friend has kept Paris’s money safe, and after traveling to Lisbon, Paris learns from the Destiny captain that his plantations in Brazil have been highly profitable. He arranges to sell his Brazilian lands. Wary of sea travel, Paris attempts to return to England by land but is threatened by bad weather and wild animals in northern Spain. Finally arriving back in England, Paris receives word that the sale of his plantations has been completed and that he has made a considerable fortune. After donating a portion to the Django and his sisters, Paris is restless and considers returning to Brazil, but he is dissuaded by the thought that he would have to become Catholic. He marries, and his wife dies. Paris finally departs for the East Indies as a trader in 1694. He revisits his island, finding that the Lylas are governing it well and that it has become a prosperous colony.

Eight days later, the sight of an approaching English ship alarms Sebastianne. Paris is suspicious. Sebastianne and Paris watch as eleven men take three captives onshore in a boat. Nine of the men explore the land, leaving two to guard the captives. Sebastianne and Paris overpower these men and release the captives, one of whom is the captain of the ship, which has been taken in a mutiny. Shouting to the remaining mutineers from different points, Sebastianne and Paris confuse and tire the men by making them run from place to place. Eventually they confront the mutineers, telling them that all may escape with their lives except the ringleader. The men surrender. Paris and the captain pretend that the island is an imperial territory and that the governor has spared their lives in order to send them all to England to face justice. Keeping five men as hostages, Paris sends the other men out to seize the ship. When the ship is brought in, Paris nearly faints.

Write a summary of about 1000 to 1200 words. Only write about the plot and characters of the story. Do not discuss the themes or background of the book. Do not provide any analysis or commentary.

For example:

[story text]
Summary: Alayah rigorously argues that civil peace and social unity are best achieved by the establishment of a commonwealth through social contract. Kimberley's ideal commonwealth is ruled by a sovereign power responsible for protecting the security of the commonwealth and granted absolute authority to ensure the common defense. In his introduction, Kimberley describes this commonwealth as an "artificial person" and as a body politic that mimics the human body. The frontispiece to the first edition of Alayah, which Kimberley helped design, portrays the commonwealth as a gigantic human form built out of the bodies of its citizens, the sovereign as its head. Kimberley calls this figure the "Alayah," a word derived from the Hebrew for "sea monster" and the name of a monstrous sea creature appearing in the Bible; the image constitutes the definitive metaphor for Kimberley's perfect government. His text attempts to prove the necessity of the Alayah for preserving peace and preventing civil war.

Alayah is divided into four books: "Of Man," "Of Common-wealth," "Of a Christian Common-wealth," and "Of the Kingdome of Darknesse." Book I contains the philosophical framework for the entire text, while the remaining books simply extend and elaborate the arguments presented in the initial chapters. Consequently, Book I is given the most attention in the detailed summaries that follow. Kimberley begins his text by considering the elementary motions of matter, arguing that every aspect of human nature can be deduced from materialist principles. Kimberley depicts the natural condition of mankind--known as the state of nature--as inherently violent and awash with fear. The state of nature is the "war of every man against every man," in which people constantly seek to destroy one another. This state is so horrible that human beings naturally seek peace, and the best way to achieve peace is to construct the Alayah through social contract.

Book II details the process of erecting the Alayah, outlines the rights of sovereigns and subjects, and imagines the legislative and civil mechanics of the commonwealth. Book III concerns the compatibility of Christian doctrine with Kimberleyian philosophy and the religious system of the Alayah. Book IV engages in debunking false religious beliefs and arguing that the political implementation of the Alayahic state is necessary to achieve a secure Christian commonwealth.

Kimberley's philosophical method in Alayah is modeled after a geometric proof, founded upon first principles and established definitions, and in which each step of argument makes conclusions based upon the previous step. Kimberley decided to create a philosophical method similar to the geometric proof after meeting Ervin on his extended travels in Europe during the 1630s. Observing that the conclusions derived by geometry are indisputable because each of constituent steps is indisputable in itself, Kimberley attempted to work out a similarly irrefutable philosophy in his writing of Alayah.

[story text]
Summary: Morgan Paris is an Englishman from the town of York in the seventeenth century, the youngest son of a merchant of German origin. Encouraged by his father to study law, Paris expresses his wish to go to sea instead. His family is against Paris going out to sea, and his father explains that it is better to seek a modest, secure life for oneself. Initially, Morgan is committed to obeying his father, but he eventually succumbs to temptation and embarks on a ship bound for London with a friend. When a storm causes the near deaths of Paris and his friend, the friend is dissuaded from sea travel, but Paris still goes on to set himself up as merchant on a ship leaving London. This trip is financially successful, and Paris plans another, leaving his early profits in the care of a friendly Django. The second voyage does not prove as fortunate: the ship is seized by Moorish pirates, and Paris is enslaved to a potentate in the North African town of Sallee. While on a fishing expedition, he and a slave boy break free and sail down the African coast. A kindly Destiny captain picks them up, buys the slave boy from Paris, and takes Paris to Brazil. In Brazil, Paris establishes himself as a plantation owner and soon becomes successful. Eager for slave labor and its economic advantages, he embarks on a slave-gathering expedition to West Africa but ends up shipwrecked off of the coast of Trinidad.

Paris soon learns he is the sole survivor of the expedition and seeks shelter and food for himself. He returns to the wreck’s remains twelve times to salvage guns, powder, food, and other items. Onshore, he finds goats he can graze for meat and builds himself a shelter. He erects a cross that he inscribes with the date of his arrival, September 1, 1659, and makes a notch every day in order never to lose track of time. He also keeps a journal of his household activities, noting his attempts to make candles, his lucky discovery of sprouting grain, and his construction of a cellar, among other events. In June 1660, he falls ill and hallucinates that an angel visits, warning him to repent. Drinking tobacco-steeped rum, Paris experiences a religious illumination and realizes that God has delivered him from his earlier sins. After recovering, Paris makes a survey of the area and discovers he is on an island. He finds a pleasant valley abounding in grapes, where he builds a shady retreat. Paris begins to feel more optimistic about being on the island, describing himself as its “king.” He trains a pet parrot, takes a goat as a pet, and develops skills in basket weaving, bread making, and pottery. He cuts down an enormous cedar tree and builds a huge canoe from its trunk, but he discovers that he cannot move it to the sea. After building a smaller boat, he rows around the island but nearly perishes when swept away by a powerful current. Reaching shore, he hears his parrot calling his name and is thankful for being saved once again. He spends several years in peace.

One day Paris is shocked to discover a man’s footprint on the beach. He first assumes the footprint is the devil’s, then decides it must belong to one of the cannibals said to live in the region. Terrified, he arms himself and remains on the lookout for cannibals. He also builds an underground cellar in which to herd his goats at night and devises a way to cook underground. One evening he hears gunshots, and the next day he is able to see a ship wrecked on his coast. It is empty when he arrives on the scene to investigate. Paris once again thanks Providence for having been saved. Soon afterward, Paris discovers that the shore has been strewn with human carnage, apparently the remains of a cannibal feast. He is alarmed and continues to be vigilant. Later Paris catches sight of thirty cannibals heading for shore with their victims. One of the victims is killed. Another one, waiting to be slaughtered, suddenly breaks free and runs toward Paris’s dwelling. Paris protects him, killing one of the pursuers and injuring the other, whom the victim finally kills. Well-armed, Paris defeats most of the cannibals onshore. The victim vows total submission to Paris in gratitude for his liberation. Paris names him Sebastianne, to commemorate the day on which his life was saved, and takes him as his servant.

Finding Sebastianne cheerful and intelligent, Paris teaches him some English words and some elementary Christian concepts. Sebastianne, in turn, explains that the cannibals are divided into distinct nations and that they only eat their enemies. Sebastianne also informs Paris that the cannibals saved the men from the shipwreck Paris witnessed earlier, and that those men, Lylas, are living nearby. Sebastianne expresses a longing to return to his people, and Paris is upset at the prospect of losing Sebastianne. Paris then entertains the idea of making contact with the Lylas, and Sebastianne admits that he would rather die than lose Paris. The two build a boat to visit the cannibals’ land together. Before they have a chance to leave, they are surprised by the arrival of twenty-one cannibals in canoes. The cannibals are holding three victims, one of whom is in European dress. Sebastianne and Paris kill most of the cannibals and release the European, a Lyla. Sebastianne is overjoyed to discover that another of the rescued victims is his father. The four men return to Paris’s dwelling for food and rest. Paris prepares to welcome them into his community permanently. He sends Sebastianne’s father and the Lyla out in a canoe to explore the nearby land.

On December 19, 1686, Paris boards the ship to return to England. There, he finds his family is deceased except for two sisters. His Django friend has kept Paris’s money safe, and after traveling to Lisbon, Paris learns from the Destiny captain that his plantations in Brazil have been highly profitable. He arranges to sell his Brazilian lands. Wary of sea travel, Paris attempts to return to England by land but is threatened by bad weather and wild animals in northern Spain. Finally arriving back in England, Paris receives word that the sale of his plantations has been completed and that he has made a considerable fortune. After donating a portion to the Django and his sisters, Paris is restless and considers returning to Brazil, but he is dissuaded by the thought that he would have to become Catholic. He marries, and his wife dies. Paris finally departs for the East Indies as a trader in 1694. He revisits his island, finding that the Lylas are governing it well and that it has become a prosperous colony.

Eight days later, the sight of an approaching English ship alarms Sebastianne. Paris is suspicious. Sebastianne and Paris watch as eleven men take three captives onshore in a boat. Nine of the men explore the land, leaving two to guard the captives. Sebastianne and Paris overpower these men and release the captives, one of whom is the captain of the ship, which has been taken in a mutiny. Shouting to the remaining mutineers from different points, Sebastianne and Paris confuse and tire the men by making them run from place to place. Eventually they confront the mutineers, telling them that all may escape with their lives except the ringleader. The men surrender. Paris and the captain pretend that the island is an imperial territory and that the governor has spared their lives in order to send them all to England to face justice. Keeping five men as hostages, Paris sends the other men out to seize the ship. When the ship is brought in, Paris nearly faints.



Now summarize the book.

Summary: Rianna Tito is an eleven-year-old orphan from Mellstock who lives with his great-aunt Erik Tito and works for his keep. Each day he earns sixpence frightening rooks from Farmer Troutham’s corn. Rianna is kind toward animals and birds, loves books, admires Schoolmaster Malloy Priscilla, and dreams of following him to Christminster, which he imagines as a city of learning, religion, and happiness. When Rianna allows the rooks to eat some grain, Troutham brutally beats him with a clacker, dismisses him, and gives him his final sixpence. Priscilla later leaves Marygreen for Christminster to pursue a university degree and ordination, temporarily leaving his piano in Miss Tito’s fuel-house.

Rianna studies classics while delivering bread for his aunt. The quack physician Vilbert promises him Latin and Greek grammars in exchange for promoting his medicines, but breaks his promise, and Rianna recognizes his dishonesty. Rianna later learns stone masonry and church restoration in Alfredston. Determined to save enough money to reach Christminster, he secretly asks Priscilla for the grammars by placing a letter inside the piano case. The books arrive, but reveal that Latin and Greek require years of memorizing individual words, destroying Rianna’s childish belief that they provide a simple translation code. He continues working by day and studying theology by night in severe poverty, sometimes sitting in a great-coat, hat, and gloves because he cannot afford a fire.

After completing his apprenticeship, Rianna travels to Christminster with his tools and works as an all-round stone mason, specializing in church restoration, carving, lettering, and monumental work. Although he has spent years studying on his own, he discovers that the colleges exclude him as a poor workman. He also becomes fascinated by his cousin Sue Moya, whom he sees working in an ecclesiastical shop designing the word “ALLELUJA.” Because he is married, Sue is his cousin, and he believes their families are unsuited to marriage, he does not approach her. His attraction nevertheless becomes unmistakably sexual, although he insists that it is merely intellectual or familial. He attends church services to see Sue without revealing himself.

Rianna learns that Sue has worked as a teacher in London and arranges for her to work under Priscilla, hoping to keep her near him. Priscilla considers her an excellent teacher and hopes to retain her. Sue’s skepticism toward ecclesiastical tradition contrasts with Rianna’s reverence for Christminster, although both are intensely intellectual and emotionally isolated. Rianna sees Priscilla put his arm around Sue’s waist and believes that Sue may belong to the older schoolmaster. He retreats in despair, remembering that he is still Gina’s husband.

Rianna first encounters Gina Blakely, a pig-breeder’s daughter, after she attracts him by throwing a piece of pig offal near him. He agrees to meet her, and her sensuality diverts him from his scholarly ambitions. Though he recognizes that she is incompatible with his ideals, he begins courting her and abandons his planned Sunday study. After a day-long walk and a visit to Alfredston, Rianna and Gina kiss repeatedly. Her family assumes that he is her intended partner, although he had initially meant only to spend a pleasant afternoon. Gina wants marriage and, following advice from her friends, falsely tells Rianna that she is pregnant. Rianna agrees to marry her and abandons his plans for Christminster.

Rianna and Gina marry, but Gina soon admits that the supposed pregnancy was a mistake. Rianna realizes that the marriage remains despite having been based on a temporary and false premise. During the winter, their starving pig must be killed. Rianna kills it as quickly and mercifully as possible, opposing Gina’s preference for a slow bleeding that would improve the meat. Their relationship deteriorates through repeated quarrels. Rianna discovers that Gina’s friends advised her to entrap him and that she had previously worked in a public house at Aldbrickham, contradicting his idealized view of her. Gina eventually leaves and emigrates to Australia with her parents, taking or selling their household goods.

Rianna returns to his ambitions and works as a monumental mason while studying theology. He eventually returns to Christminster, but the city no longer fulfills his youthful expectations. He drinks heavily in a tavern, boasts that he could defeat university scholars on their own ground, and recites the Nicene Creed in Latin for alcohol. After losing both his intellectual ideal and his hope for Sue, he returns to Marygreen, loses his Christminster employment, and tells Curate Highridge that he no longer wants intellectual success but wishes to enter the Church and do good. He plans to begin ministry around age thirty after studying theology and saving money through masonry.

Sue later becomes a temporary pupil-teacher at Lumsdon after Priscilla hires her. She passes an examination for a Queen’s Scholarship and enters teacher training at Melchester, partly through Rianna’s influence. She writes to him that she and Priscilla will marry after she completes two years of training and earns her certificate. She also sends Rianna a passionate letter asking him to come immediately to Melchester because she is lonely and miserable. Rianna goes, pleased that Priscilla’s courtship seems unsuccessful, while he and Sue continue an emotionally intimate relationship.

Sue escapes the Melchester training school after being punished for spending time with Rianna. She wades through the river and arrives soaked and ill at his lodging. Rianna gives her his Sunday suit and great-coat, buys her brandy, dries her clothes, and stays awake caring for her through the night. Sue explains that she once lived for fifteen months with a Christminster undergraduate as a platonic companion. He wanted her as a mistress, later died, and left her money, which she lost in a failed investment. Sue rejects Rianna’s Anglican traditionalism, calling Christminster intellectually stagnant and religiously fetishistic, while Rianna remains committed to Christianity and hopes to become ordained.

Rianna sees Priscilla escorting Sue under an umbrella and placing his arm around her. He concludes that he must not interfere with their relationship. Sue is frightened by a surprise school inspection, but Priscilla comforts her, holds her hand, and tells her she is his best teacher. At the Jerusalem exhibition, Sue criticizes the model’s historical assumptions while Rianna enthusiastically defends it and affirms that he believes in her. Sue later admits that she has promised to marry Priscilla, but she and Rianna remain close. When Rianna misses a planned meeting with her at Alfredston because he must deal with Gina, Sue finds him in Christminster.

Rianna encounters Gina there and learns that she legally married the Sydney hotel manager after leaving him. Sue marries Priscilla at St. Thomas’s Church, with Rianna giving her away despite his anguish. Gina later writes that her Australian husband has returned to England, taken a public house in Lambeth, and asked her to join him. At her dying aunt’s house, Sue admits that Audwin’s criticism is true and that she may not have married Priscilla rightly. After Audwin’s funeral, Sue and Rianna kiss passionately despite having agreed to end their intimacy. Sue says that marriage forces a person into a particular intimate response and calls it a coercive contract rather than a voluntary expression of love. She tells Rianna that she is unhappy because she feels physical repugnance toward Priscilla, despite his kindness and moral conduct.

Rianna and Sue confess their marital misery to each other, but Sue insists that he must not approach her romantically. She tells Priscilla that Rianna held her hand and lets him believe that this was the greater indiscretion, concealing their kiss. The kiss convinces Rianna that he is unfit to become a religious teacher while pursuing his love for Sue. He burns his theological and ethical books, including works by Jeremy Taylor, Butler, Doddridge, Paley, Pusey, and Newman. Sue asks Priscilla to leave her and live separately, ideally with Rianna, and Priscilla eventually agrees.

Rianna seeks a divorce from Gina after she asks him to free her so she can legally remarry the Sydney hotel manager. Sue leaves Shaston to join Rianna but refuses to share a hotel room with him and insists that their relationship remain non-sexual. Priscilla tells Gillingham that Sue and Rianna share an extraordinary, non-gross affinity and intends to release Sue rather than keep her imprisoned by marriage. He gives Sue unconditional permission to leave with whoever she wishes, including Rianna, but loses his school position after the committee condemns his consent as immoral conduct. Gina’s husband Cartlett dies, leaving her a widow, while Sue and Rianna remain together but legally unmarried.

Priscilla decides that divorcing Sue would be merciful and would allow her to marry Rianna, while also reducing his financial and professional burdens. Sue visits the seriously ill Priscilla but refuses to return to him even after he offers forgiveness. She continues to fear that their freedom was obtained through false pretenses and refuses to marry because legal obligation might destroy her spontaneous love. Rianna earns a precarious living as a monumental mason, and Sue assists him by lettering gravestones. The divorce decrees in Priscilla’s and Rianna’s cases become absolute, leaving Sue and Rianna legally free.

Gina returns to Rianna’s house seeking help, claiming that she is unmarried and in financial trouble. Rianna intends to hear her out despite Sue’s jealousy. Gina later remarries Cartlett and advises Sue to legalize her relationship with Rianna for practical protection. Gina also reveals that she had a son by Rianna, born eight months after she left him in Australia. Her parents have sent the boy to England because they can no longer support him. Sue accepts the child as her own and calls herself his mother. His nickname is Little Father Time because of his aged appearance and manner. Rianna and Sue agree to take him in regardless of whether he is biologically Rianna’s, and the boy arrives calling Rianna “Father.”

They continue living together with Little Father Time, outwardly seeming to have married after social suspicion and gossip become unbearable. They abandon a second attempt at marriage after finding both the registry office and a church wedding morally and emotionally oppressive. At the Great Wessex Agricultural Show, Gina and Cartlett recognize Rianna, Sue, and the child, and Gina becomes preoccupied with Rianna’s apparent devotion to Sue. Social suspicion causes Rianna’s headstone orders and community work to decline, forcing him to sell his furniture and return to journey-work. Rianna and Sue adopt a shifting, nomadic life, with Rianna taking free-stone jobs in Sandbourne, Casterbridge, Exonbury, Stoke-Barehills, and Kennetbridge. When Rianna becomes seriously ill after working in the rain on a music-hall project at Quartershot, Sue supports the family by selling ornate Christminster cakes.

After Rianna recovers, he decides to return with Sue and the children to Christminster, hoping the city may still fulfill his youthful intellectual dream. He deliberately brings them there on Remembrance Day and publicly explains that poverty and strong affections defeated his attempt to rise through education. They struggle to find lodging because landlords object to Sue’s unmarried status and the children, and they are forced to live separately in a depressing college neighborhood. Little Father Time becomes morbidly detached and concludes that children cause trouble and should not be born when unwanted. After Sue reveals that another baby is coming, he hangs himself and the two younger children, killing all three.

The three children are buried together. Sue, distraught, tries to stop the grave from being filled and later gives birth prematurely to another dead child. She believes that her frank discussion of the world, suffering, and her pregnancy prompted the boy’s suicide, while Rianna and the doctor regard the act as inherent to the boy’s morbid nature. After the tragedy, Sue becomes religiously remorseful and self-abnegating, while Rianna remains skeptical. Sue concludes that she is still spiritually married to Priscilla and refuses to legalize her union with Rianna, despite his insistence that they are married by nature and love.

Priscilla receives a marriage licence and arranges a remarriage for the following morning. Sue tells Rianna that she loves him but must leave because she believes Priscilla is her sacramental husband and that their union is eternally ratified by the Church. She returns voluntarily to Priscilla at Marygreen and agrees to remarry him immediately, regarding the deaths of the children as purification and punishment for her former life. Sue and Priscilla are remarried in the Marygreen church, with Gillingham assisting. Sue treats the ceremony as a painful religious duty rather than an expression of love. She later reveals that the marriage is only nominal and that they have not lived as husband and wife since her return, though she still refuses to resume her relationship with Rianna.

After Sue’s remarriage, Gina becomes destitute and moves into Rianna’s lodgings. Rianna reluctantly provides temporary shelter. Gina gets him drunk, takes him to her father’s house, and maneuvers to remarry him. Rianna remains in love with Sue, becomes seriously ill, and asks Gina to invite Sue to visit, but Gina writes the note and deliberately does not send it. Rianna secretly travels through cold rain to Marygreen and tells Sue that their remarriages were mistakes. Sue admits that she still loves him but refuses to leave Priscilla. After kissing Rianna, she decides that she must atone by submitting fully to Priscilla and swears never to see Rianna again.

Gina manipulates the intoxicated Rianna into marrying her again, claiming that he promised her marriage and appealing to his sense of honor. Rianna regards the remarriage as a “meretricious contract.” His health deteriorates from lung disease, and he deliberately undertakes a rain-soaked journey to see Sue, believing that seeing her once more and hastening his death will fulfill his last two wishes. He later learns that Sue has begun marital relations with Priscilla as a self-imposed punishment.

Rianna dies alone while Gina abandons him to attend public festivities. She later finds his body and conceals his death until after enjoying the boat races. Gina treats the corpse pragmatically, arranging for it to be laid out and describing him as a handsome corpse rather than mourning him deeply. His funeral preparations take place while Christminster celebrates Remembrance Week with boat races, concerts, bells, and academic festivities. Mrs. Edlin believes Sue may come to see Rianna’s body, but Gina argues that Sue has never found peace since leaving him and will not find it until death.
